Wireframe

You might say

Hold off on colors—sketch a gray page skeleton first: header, hero, three cards, footer, just the positions.

A wireframe is the page skeleton drawn in gray blocks and placeholder lines—it fixes "what goes where" before any colors or fonts.·Sketch the page in gray blocks first: how tall the header is, what sits in the hero, where the button goes. With positions settled, colors and fonts can be adjusted without reworking the layout. The wireframe fixes positions; the visual design handles colors and fonts.

The wireframe stage confirms positions; changes only move boxesSkeleton first, skin second—rework costs least.
What the wireframe owns

Positions and sizes: Header height, hero footprint, card arrangement—structure questions get settled here, and changes only move boxes.

Placeholder text: Until real copy exists, label blocks as "one headline" or "one paragraph" instead of inventing content for the skeleton.

What it is not

A wireframe is not a visual mockup: no colors, fonts, or images, so don't judge it by looks. It is also not a requirements doc—requirements say "for whom and what," the wireframe says "where." With an AI, split the rounds: confirm structure on the wireframe, then ask for visuals.
